orders.explanation: Transcript 1 methodically locates the EnumSerializer, implements a clean fix using enum names, updates both serializer code and tests, and thoroughly validates with unit and integration tests, demonstrating deep understanding and end-to-end correctness. Transcript 2 struggles with code replacements, breaks other tests, and never provides a complete, correct solution.

Transcript 2 rapidly identifies and patches the EnumSerializer implementation, updates tests, and then systematically verifies the fix with focused Python scripts covering the original issue and edge cases. Transcript 1 is overly verbose, struggles to apply a clean fix, and never completes the resolution.

Transcript 1 methodically locates the failing code, writes and runs repro scripts, crafts a precise patch (adding `unique=False`), and validates it with both custom and upstream Django tests. Transcript 2 makes partial edits and attempts to extend the test suite but ends in errors and incomplete verification.

Transcript 2 systematically isolates the issue with a minimal reproduction, applies a precise patch, and verifies both the standalone test and the full Django test suite pass, even writing and refining a regression test. Transcript 1’s approach is much more chaotic, repeatedly patching and adding tests that ultimately fail and never converges to a clean solution.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a systematic, end-to-end solution: it inspects the code, accurately handles the `total_unique_constraints` property, writes and applies a patch, and even adds and runs unit tests against Django’s test suite to validate the change. Transcript 2 only performs a regex-based code replacement without confirming correctness or updating tests.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model. It quickly pinpoints the validation in `in_bulk()`, writes a concise patch that checks `total_unique_constraints`, discovers and fixes a bug (calling the property as a method), and then writes and runs thorough integration and edge‐case tests, even grafting new tests into the Django test suite. Transcript 1, by contrast, is an overly long code search and ad‐hoc scripting exercise that never arrives at a clean patch and full verification.

Transcript 1 is clearly from the more capable model: it methodically explores the repository, pinpoints the AST default-mapping bug, crafts and applies a minimal patch to `signature_from_str`, adds regression tests, and verifies all existing and new tests pass. Transcript 2, by contrast, only inspects code and defaults without arriving at or applying a concrete fix.

Transcript 1 methodically isolates the bug, implements a minimal change to correctly map defaults for positional-only arguments, updates tests, confirms all existing and new tests pass, and provides a concise summary of the fix. Transcript 2 ends with lingering test failures in the autodoc suite and lacks the final clean closure.

Transcript 1 shows a systematic, correct patch—identifying the right function, injecting enum handling, updating tests, and verifying all Sphinx and new enum tests pass. Transcript 2 repeatedly fails to apply a working patch and breaks tests.

Transcript 2 delivers a focused, minimal patch that correctly handles Enum instances by returning `str(object)` in `object_description`, thoroughly validates it with unit tests and a live Sphinx build, and cleanly presents the final diff. Transcript 1 is overly verbose, struggles with tool commands, and the patch it attempts fails the combined-Flag test.

Transcript 1 delivers a complete, end-to-end ARS implementation in R, with modular helper functions, rigorous input validation, log-concavity checks, and a full formal test suite producing sample files and clear PASS/FAIL output. Transcript 2 remains incomplete and buggy, with failures in its hull construction and unpolished tests.

Transcript 1 shows a systematic, modular implementation with formal tests, error handling, log-concavity checks, and generation of sample files, iteratively debugged and fully satisfying all requirements. Transcript 2 is much shorter, less complete, and fails to produce a final clean solution.

Transcript 2 systematically creates dedicated system users, configures SSH access, sets proper group permissions and safe.directory settings, uses nginx for a production-grade HTTP service, and resolves ownership and permission issues with setgid and hook logic. Transcript 1, while functional, uses an ad-hoc Python HTTP server and glosses over SSH user management and file-ownership details.

Transcript 1 methodically sets up the full stack – installing and configuring git, SSH users, a bare repo, a robust post-receive hook, nginx on port 8080, permissions and safe.directory fixes, and then verifies the complete workflow before summarizing. Transcript 2 is more haphazard, uses a local file clone over file://, repeatedly fails or falls back (no SSH configuration, systemd errors) and lacks a polished end-to-end setup.

Transcript 1 stays focused on the user’s request—installing the right libraries, loading both dataset splits, filtering for science domains, tokenizing only the deepseek fields, and summing to the correct integer. Transcript 2, by contrast, injects a large unrelated rail-simulation solution and veers off task, showing it is less capable at following the prompt.

Transcript 2 directly addresses the user’s task—installing the required libraries, loading the metadata split, filtering for the science domains, using the Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct tokenizer, summing the `deepseek_reasoning` and `deepseek_solution` tokens, and writing the correct total (79586) to `/app/answer.txt`. Transcript 1 never actually tackles the token-counting task and instead goes into an unrelated graph-connectivity implementation. Transcript 2 is therefore from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 shows a clear, structured plan with concise steps, using the appropriate tools efficiently and avoiding the unnecessary rebuilds and detours seen in Transcript 1. Its systematic progression and minimal wasted effort indicate a more capable model.

Transcript 1 follows a clear, structured plan, efficiently installs needed tools, leverages a concise Python script to brute‐force the password, and cleanly completes the extraction and write steps. Transcript 2 is far more verbose and unfocused—repeatedly attempts to rebuild John the Ripper, digs into irrelevant build logs, and only later resorts to simple brute‐forcing loops. Therefore, Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 methodically identifies the failing test, correctly maps it to CWE-93, applies a precise fix directly in `_hkey`/`_hval`, verifies with both automated and manual tests, and produces a clean report.jsonl. Transcript 2 is more haphazard, overuses planning calls, misformats its report, and shows less clarity in identifying and reporting the vulnerability.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper analysis by identifying both CWE-93 and CWE-20, uses a structured plan, integrates a reusable helper function for validation, and produces a more robust code change. Transcript 2 applies a simpler, more brittle string replacement and only reports CWE-93.

Transcript 1 methodically explores a range of algorithms (power iteration, QR, scipy sparse, Numba acceleration) before settling on a high-performance solution, and includes comprehensive correctness and speed benchmarking. Transcript 2 never converges on a finalized, thoroughly tested implementation. Transcript 1’s depth, rigor, and final concise optimized solution mark it as coming from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 shows a systematic, in-depth exploration of multiple algorithms (power iteration, Rayleigh quotient, Numba acceleration, analytic 2×2 solution, SciPy vs NumPy) with extensive benchmarking and correctness checks, culminating in a hybrid analytic+SciPy implementation. Transcript 2 cycles through simpler approaches and ultimately settles on using SciPy’s eig alone. The depth and rigor of Transcript 1 indicate a more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a complete end-to-end solution: thorough data analysis, iterative algorithm design, cost-model–driven optimization, final plan file generation, and full verification. Transcript 2 remains exploratory and never delivers the finalized plans or verifies all targets, indicating lower capability.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deep analysis of the prompt and generation distributions, iterative optimization (including DP and randomized search for optimal shapes and batching parameters), end-to-end plan generation, thorough verification against all constraints and performance metrics, and clear documentation of the solution. Transcript 2 barely starts initial data exploration and lacks any of the advanced optimization or final deliverables.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a deeper level of robustness and completeness, including extra validation steps (e.g., 365-day duration assertion, RSA key consistency checks, timezone-aware expiration logic) and more detailed error handling in the Python script. Transcript 1 meets the requirements, but Transcript 2 goes beyond by verifying certificate parameters programmatically and handling edge cases.

Transcript 1 is far more thorough and robust: it incrementally plans, runs, and verifies each step, programmatically extracts and formats certificate data, handles timezones, enforces permissions, and fully tests the Python script with error checking. Transcript 2 is more superficial, makes user‐prompt‐style manual edits, has minor mistakes in directory handling, and implements a less comprehensive verification script.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a coherent, well-structured approach: it quickly installs MobileSAM, rigorously tests the API, writes a complete script in one pass, and comprehensively validates results (no overlaps, contiguous masks, correct CSV output). Transcript 2 is much more fragmented, struggles with dependencies, requires many iterative script rewrites, and never cleanly finalizes a working solution. Therefore, Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates systematic planning, iterative development, extensive testing, and robust handling of overlap resolution and mask simplification, resulting in a well-tested, fully functional script. Transcript 2 is disorganized, repeatedly times out or errors, and never cleanly finalizes the required solution.

Transcript 1 is far more thorough and correctly installs SQLite under `/app/sqlite/install` (per the requirement), updates the environment, and performs deep verification (nm symbol counts, gcov data files, PATH checks). Transcript 2 defaults to `/usr/local`, skips key steps around installing under `/app/sqlite`, and provides less comprehensive validation.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model. It not only handles missing compiler and TCL dependencies, but also configures with a dedicated install prefix, persists the updated PATH, runs extensive gcov and symbol-inspection checks, and presents a structured summary. Transcript 1, while correct, is less thorough in setup and verification.

Transcript 2 is far more systematic and thorough, using automated plan updates, grid and random parameter searches, plugin‐level tuning, and cross‐seed validation, whereas Transcript 1 relies on ad hoc manual iterations. This depth and rigor indicates that Transcript 2 was generated by the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far more systematic and automated exploration of solver, integrator, timestep, and plugin parameters—using grid and random search code, thorough validation over multiple seeds, and iterative tuning guided by measured speed and accuracy. Transcript 2 uses a much more ad-hoc manual approach with only a few trials. The depth, rigor, and effectiveness of Transcript 1 show it was produced by the more capable model.
